title: Iterative divider off ALU critical path
motivation:
The baseline timing report shows the worst path entering the EX forwarding
muxes and then the monolithic ALU. The current ALU keeps RV32M DIV/REM in
the same combinational result mux as ADD, branch compare support, and memory
address generation, so every common integer operation pays timing for a rare
slow operation. CoreMark's hot path is dominated by simple ALU, load/store,
and branch work, making the divider a high-value target for a focused
timing micro-optimization.

Move DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU out of the combinational ALU and into a small
iterative divide/remainder unit controlled by EX. Keep ADD/SUB/logic/shift,
compare, multiply, load/store address, and jump return generation on the
existing single-cycle path, but assert an EX-local stall only while a divide
or remainder instruction is in flight. Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS, preserve
the existing combinational substitute formulas so the fast formal checks keep
their current behavior. Removing the divider cone from the normal ALU mux
should substantially improve Fmax while adding cycles only for rare RV32M
division instructions.

title: Multicycle M-extension unit off ALU path
motivation:
The baseline timing report shows the critical path running through the
forwarding muxes, EX-stage ALU, and back into the EX/MEM register, with
the RV32M multiplier/divider logic present in the same combinational ALU
cone as ordinary ADD/SUB/branch address work. That structure forces every
non-M instruction to pay timing for rare or moderately frequent M-extension
operations, limiting Fmax far more than the simple five-stage pipeline
should on Tang Nano 20K.

higher Fmax while only adding cycles on actual M-extension instructions.

title: Static direct-control-flow predictor
motivation:
The current five-stage core resolves every branch and jump in EX, then flushes
the younger IF and ID work on any taken redirect. CoreMark has many loop-back
branches and direct calls/jumps, so paying the full redirect penalty on every
taken direct control-flow instruction leaves meaningful iterations/cycle on
the table even if Fmax is unchanged. A very small predictor should improve IPC
without touching the existing critical ALU/forwarding path.

title: Valid-predicated load-use interlock
motivation:
After moving DIV/REM out of the single-cycle ALU, the best timing report no
longer points at arithmetic. The new worst path runs from the register file
through ID/EX, EX redirect/fetch control, hazard control, and back into the
ID/EX register enable/data mux. The current fetch path also injects a wide
NOP instruction on redirect or imem stall, and the load-use interlock
compares both raw instruction source fields even when rs2 is actually an
immediate bitfield. That is a good micro-optimization target because it is
on the hot control path and can create false CoreMark bubbles.

title: Registered IF/ID control boundary
motivation:
After the iterative divider improvement, the timed critical path is no
longer dominated by RV32M arithmetic. The reported worst path now loops
through decode, execute redirect generation, fetch flush selection, the
hazard unit, and back into the ID/EX register enable/data mux. The current
IF/ID payload is combinational, so branch redirect, imem stall, load-use
detection, and ID/EX capture all sit in one broad control cone.

title: Tiny PC-indexed BTB predictor
motivation:
The previous predictor attempt showed that decoding imem_data in fetch and
adding a branch immediate target directly into the PC update path can destroy
Fmax. However, CoreMark still has enough loop branches and direct control
transfers that avoiding EX redirect bubbles is attractive if the prediction
path is kept short. A predictor indexed only by the current PC should preserve
most of the champion's timing while recovering cycles on repeated taken
branches and jumps.

hypothesis.hypothesis:

predictor table cost and much lower Fmax risk than decode-time prediction.

title: Fast ADD/address ALU bypass
motivation:
The current champion's worst timing path is no longer the divider or the

feeds all non-DIV operations through one generic ALU result mux that includes
shifts, comparisons, logic, LUI, and multiply variants even when the operation
is a simple add used for memory addressing.

title: Fall-through fetch prebuffer
motivation:
The current frontend is tightly coupled to decode: an imemReady bubble makes
IF/ID invalid immediately, and a dmem stall also holds the PC so the otherwise
independent instruction bus cannot fetch ahead. With the benchmark's random
22% instruction stalls and separate instruction/data buses, CoreMark is likely
losing cycles that could be hidden by fetching sequential instructions during
backend stalls and replaying them through later imem bubbles.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational IF/ID fetch handoff with a small fall-through
prefetch FIFO, sized around four entries, that fetches ahead on io_imemReady

cycle. The PC generator remains simple and sequential, with EX redirects
flushing the FIFO and restarting fetch at the redirect target; no imem_data
decode, BTB, or prediction logic is added to the PC update path. This
structural decoupling should improve iterations per cycle by allowing fetch
to run during dmem stalls, DIV/REM busy periods, and load-use bubbles, then
absorb short random imemReady gaps without increasing the existing EX ALU
critical path.

title: Single-entry loop-back predictor
motivation:
The previous predictor attempts proved there are enough taken control-flow
bubbles in CoreMark to save roughly five percent of cycles, but they also
showed that fetch-stage immediate decode or a multi-entry BTB/BHT can crush
Fmax on Tang Nano 20K. The best predictor angle now is therefore not a more
general predictor, but the smallest predictor that attacks the hottest loop
branch case while keeping the PC update path almost as short as the current
pc+4/EX-redirect mux.

Add a one-entry loop-back branch target latch trained only by resolved taken

The prediction metadata, including the predicted target and the stored
instruction word, travels with the fetched instruction so EX can verify the
actual resolved next PC and recover on loop exits, aliases, symbolic formal
instruction changes, and misaligned traps. Correctly predicted hot loop-back
branches should avoid the current EX redirect bubble, while the hardware cost
should be far smaller than the failed static direct predictor or tiny BTB.

title: Decode precomputed PC lanes
motivation:
The current accepted core is still limited by the ID/EX-to-EX/MEM execute
region, with recent worst paths landing in or near the compact ALU result
register. Prior structural attempts show that adding predictor lookup,
wider forwarding, or extra visible stalls tends to cost more than it saves.
A safer structural target is the PC-relative work still recomputed in EX for
jumps, branch targets, and fallthrough bookkeeping even though it depends
only on the fetch PC and immediate already available in decode.

title: Tagless loop target predictor
motivation: Prior predictor attempts show that CoreMark has enough taken loop and direct-JAL traffic to save cycles, but exact tags, fetch-time immediate decode, RAS state, or predicted-target payloads repeatedly erased the gain in Fmax. The closest designs carried only a one-bit predicted-taken marker, yet still paid for a full-PC tag match and target selection in IF. A predictor that drops the tag compare entirely may keep most of the loop-cycle win with a much shorter lookup cone.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a very small tagless direct-mapped target cache, for example four flop-backed entries indexed by low PC bits, trained only by resolved taken backward conditional branches and direct JALs. Each entry stores valid, aligned target, and a 2-bit confidence counter, but no full PC tag. IF predicts taken only when the indexed entry is valid and strongly taken, selects the stored target, and carries a single predicted_taken bit through IF/ID and ID/EX; it does not decode imem_data, carry a predicted target, or compare full tags.

EX keeps correctness by suppressing the normal redirect only when a predicted_taken instruction is actually a taken direct branch or JAL. If the tagless entry aliases a non-control instruction, a forward/not-taken branch, a loop exit, JALR, or a trapping/misaligned instruction, EX redirects to the architectural next PC using the existing flush path and weakens/clears the indexed entry. This deliberately accepts occasional alias recoveries to remove the full-PC compare and wide verification metadata that hurt previous predictors, aiming for a net CoreMark gain from hot loop branches.
